sections.html:
Union County takes up about 515 square miles in the upstate and shares borders with Cherokee, York, Chester, Fairfield, Newberry, Laurens and Spartanburg counties. A slice of Sumter National Forest sits within it. Its seat is the city of Union, home to 8,174 people in 2020.

Health care is now the biggest employment sector, at about 21.7 percent. Milliken & Company, Sonoco, Walmart, Timken and Dollar General rank among the big employers. Textile plants once dominated, then mostly closed or moved overseas during the 1980s and 1990s.

sections.h2: Older neighborhoods and old family land
sections.html:
Three areas are on the National Register of Historic Places: East Main Street-Douglass Heights, South Street-South Church Street, and Union Downtown. An owner inside one should phone the county before starting outside work, to learn whether local rules apply.

Plenty of land here stays in one family for generations, and county lines have shifted more than once, with two townships going to Cherokee County in 1897. Old deeds may name places and neighbors long gone. On inherited acreage, a title company should check where the records sit and who is entitled to sign before a contract is signed.

The work is split among four county offices, each with a separate phone.

OfficeHandlesPhone
AssessorValues real property, about 22,000 parcels(864) 429-1650
AuditorTax bills, homestead exemptions, personal property(864) 429-1618
TreasurerTax payments(864) 429-1606
Delinquent Tax CollectorOverdue taxes and the tax sale(864) 429-1617

Find the Assessor at 203 West Main Street, Union, SC 29379, open 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday, holidays excepted. Delinquent Tax is in the same building and starts half an hour earlier, at 8:30. The courthouse itself is 210 W. Main Street. Plants, railroads and utilities are valued by the state Department of Revenue rather than the Assessor.

The 2025 countywide reappraisal values property as of December 31, 2024, and the 2024 taxable value carries forward for four more years, barring a few listed exceptions. State law calls for a new reappraisal every five years.

  • That valuation and classification notice is not a tax bill.
  • Any shift of $1,000 or more in value or classification must be reported to you by the county.
  • Mill levies are set annually, so your bill can move even when assessed value stays flat.
  • A missing tax notice doesn't change the tax, penalty, interest, due date or lien.

Send the Assessor your up-to-date mailing address in writing. Agricultural land switched to another use triggers rollback taxes covering this year and the three before.

Filing inside 90 days of the notice date preserves all your options. The back of the valuation notice and the Assessor's website explain the steps, and an informal appeal form is online.

County Council appoints the Board of Assessment Appeals, which holds conferences on classification and real property assessment. Setting values or taxes is not its job. Its ruling can be contested by the owner or the Assessor before the Administrative Law Judge Division, with the S.C. Supreme Court as a last stop.

Filing an appeal won't stretch your payment deadline, so pay on schedule to avoid penalties and interest.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
The county's bills trail the tax year by twelve months. October brings the notices, and a payment made through January 15 is penalty-free. Later payments add 3 percent, then 10 percent after February 1, then 15 percent plus execution costs after March 16. A bill is delinquent from March 17, or the next business day.

Walk-in payers may use cash, cashier's checks, postal money orders, certified checks or Visa and Mastercard. Mail, phone and lockbox payments are taken as well. Delinquent bills can't be paid in pieces, because the county's system can't record partial payments.

South Carolina law backs the same stepped penalty and allows the treasurer to waive it for a taxpayer with clear and convincing proof of paying on time.

Parcels with unpaid taxes are auctioned in public. Anyone hoping to keep a parcel must pay before the auction, since paying later does not undo it. A sale takes place each fall; call (864) 429-1617 for the next date, how to register and what happened at the last one.

  • The Union County News carries the notice for three consecutive weeks ahead of the sale.
  • Parcels without a buyer pass to the Union County Forfeited Land Commission, which hands them out first come, first served, for cash.
  • An owner can buy a sold parcel back by paying taxes, assessments, penalties and costs, with 3, 6, 9 or 12 percent interest added.

The state's redemption window is 12 months. Ask the office how that clock applies to your parcel.

Begin with a payoff letter that includes penalties, from the Treasurer or the Delinquent Tax Collector. Check the tax map number and the recorded owner ahead of closing. A notice mailed to the previous owner may qualify for a waiver under state law, so ask. Old family land warrants a title search.

The closing agent subtracts what is owed from your proceeds, which lets the buyer take the property without the tax lien. Learn the figure early and the last week stays calm. If a sale date is near, say so to any buyer immediately.

Our company purchases Union County homes in their present state, among them inherited houses and ones with tax debt. Give us the address and the balance, and we will lay out how a cash deal might work.

sections.h2: Putting it together before you sell
sections.html:
A sale in Union County usually runs in this order. First, learn what is owed by calling the Treasurer or the Delinquent Tax Collector. Second, find out whether a valuation notice recently changed your value or classification, since a wrong figure can be appealed inside the 90-day window. Third, settle who must sign, which matters most with inherited houses. Fourth, agree on a buyer and a closing date, and let the closing agent pay off the tax from your proceeds.

Skipping the first step is the common mistake. An owner who assumes the bill was paid, then learns that a prior-year balance carries penalties and execution costs, loses time and money at the last minute. A single call early in the process avoids that, and it gives a cash buyer an honest number to work from.

Before phoning or visiting, set out the tax map number, the latest bill and any valuation notice, plus a photo ID. To claim a homestead exemption, ask the Auditor which proof is required. An appeal is stronger with evidence of value, like recent sales nearby. Copies of every filing, with dates, are worth keeping.

faqs.q: When are Union County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Penalty-free through January 15. After that the charge becomes 3 percent, then 10 percent after February 1, and 15 percent plus execution costs after March 16.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Union County assessment?
faqs.a: Ninety days from the notice date. Appealing does not push back the due date.

faqs.q: Does Union County accept partial payments on delinquent taxes?
faqs.a: No. Its bookkeeping system can't take partial payments, so the whole delinquent amount is required.

faqs.q: Who do I call about Union County property tax?
faqs.a: Values: Assessor, (864) 429-1650. Bills and exemptions: Auditor, (864) 429-1618. Payments: Treasurer, (864) 429-1606. Overdue taxes: Delinquent Tax Collector, (864) 429-1617.

faqs.q: Can I still redeem a property after a Union County tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, inside the redemption window. You owe the taxes, assessments, penalties and costs, plus interest of 3, 6, 9 or 12 percent based on timing.
